newsitem.title: ITALY: INSTANT VIEW - Italy prelim Feb CPI 0.0 pct mo/mo.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Italy prelim Feb CPI 0.0 pct mo/mo.

text.p: Following are economists' reactions to February preliminary Italian inflation data from six sample cities which analysts estimated as showing a month-on-month rate of 0.0 percent.
The year-on-year CPI rate was seen at around 2.3 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast on average a month-on-month rate of 0.2 percent and a year-on-year rate of 2.5 percent.

Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets here, said: "The data are extremely good and much better than expected by the market and they clearly show no price pressures in the economy although there are probably some exceptional factors."

Five more cities publish their inflation data on Friday and national statistics institute Istat releases final February data on March 4. Final January CPI stood at 0.2 percent month on month and 2.6 percent year on year.
The six cities weigh 41.2 percent on the national index while those remaining for Friday count for 34.4 percent.

"One of the largest exceptional factors was price discounts which have been allowed by major manufacturers. Discounts on cars had a role," De Gregorio said. "But all worries concerning a possible increase in inflation because of an ongoing rise in labour costs are probably exaggerated."

Alessandro Fugnoli, head of research at Caboto in Milan, told Reuters Financial Television: "I think tomorrow will confirm this data and for the next few months the trend will go on probably until the summer. We see a level of 1.7 to 1.8 percent between May and June."
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ in London, told RFTV he expected the Bank of Italy to keep "half an eye on the currency" before making an cuts in official interest rates.

"The Bank of Italy may well pause until we get the final inflation figures but if we see the currency stabilise they could make quite a significant rate cut on the back of this very good inflation news - towards the end of March and probably about 50 basis points."
The discount rate currently stands at 6.75 percent and was last lowered on January 22 this year.

Fugnoli said he expected a rate cut would take longer. "The strategy of the Bank of Italy is probably to bring Italian inflation to the same level as Germany this year so the next cut will be in the summer and in any case not before a credible mini budget has been approved between March and April."
"The market is looking at what the government will do. The market doesn't want any form of creative accounting, it wants a real cut in expenses," Fugnoli said.
